interpretation.summary: A simple ordinary least squares linear regression was performed with x as the predictor and y as the outcome, using 60 complete observations. The estimated slope is 0.60916, meaning y is estimated to change by that amount per one-unit increase in x, with a ninety-five percent confidence interval from -0.19622 to 1.4145. The associated p-value is 0.13545. Because this p-value is not below the five percent threshold, the evidence for a linear association between x and y is inconclusive; this does not mean there is no association, only that the data do not provide sufficient evidence of one. The interval includes the possibility of no linear relationship as well as positive and negative slopes, so the direction of any underlying linear association is not resolved. The model also includes an intercept, and the proportion of variance in y explained by the linear fit is modest. Several diagnostic warnings were carried forward: potential influential observations were flagged but none were removed, heteroscedasticity was indicated so the ordinary slope p-value and interval may be unreliable, and residual normality was flagged so ordinary slope inference requires judgement. No observations were dropped, so no complete-case deletion occurred.
limitations: The linear regression assumes a linear mean relationship, independent observations, and constant error variance; these assumptions were not established by the diagnostics.
Heteroscedasticity was flagged, so the reported slope p-value and confidence interval may be unreliable.
Residual normality was flagged, so ordinary slope inference requires judgement.
Potential influential observations were flagged and were not removed automatically, so results may be sensitive to them.
The confidence interval reflects sampling uncertainty only and does not capture model misspecification or measurement error.
This analysis does not establish causality.
No practical or clinical importance can be claimed without additional context.
The inconclusive result is not evidence that no linear association exists.
